title: Neoplasia — Classification, Invasion & Staging
source: Neoplasia Lecture Slides-1.pptx + Lecture 1 and 2 outlines

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. The outline contrasts normal regulated renewal with loss of growth control.
cards.text: Cancer is characterised by {{c1::unregulated cell proliferation}}.
cards.question: Cancer is characterised by {{c1::unregulated cell proliferation}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. Normal division in skin, gastrointestinal tissue and blood does not itself imply cancer.
cards.text: Normal cell turnover maintains a functional {{c1::steady state}}.
cards.question: Normal cell turnover maintains a functional {{c1::steady state}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. Growth-factor independence is one of the altered controls listed by the outline.
cards.text: Cancer cells may become less dependent on external {{c1::growth factors}}.
cards.question: Cancer cells may become less dependent on external {{c1::growth factors}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. The outline also lists loss of density-dependent inhibition of growth.
cards.text: Failure to stop proliferating when cells contact neighbours is loss of {{c1::contact inhibition}}.
cards.question: Failure to stop proliferating when cells contact neighbours is loss of {{c1::contact inhibition}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. Distinguish substrate attachment from contact between neighbouring cells.
cards.text: Growth without the normal requirement for attachment to a substrate is loss of {{c1::anchorage dependence}}.
cards.question: Growth without the normal requirement for attachment to a substrate is loss of {{c1::anchorage dependence}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. The outline contrasts relatively well-differentiated benign tumours with often poorly differentiated malignant tumours.
cards.text: Reduced resemblance to the specialised tissue of origin is loss of {{c1::differentiation}}.
cards.question: Reduced resemblance to the specialised tissue of origin is loss of {{c1::differentiation}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. A single universal cancer treatment or prognosis cannot be inferred from the word cancer alone.
cards.text: Cancer is a family of diseases with different treatment responses and {{c1::clinical outcomes}}.
cards.question: Cancer is a family of diseases with different treatment responses and {{c1::clinical outcomes}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. The other is the cell or tissue of origin.
cards.text: One basis for classifying neoplasms is their biological {{c1::behaviour}}.
cards.question: One basis for classifying neoplasms is their biological {{c1::behaviour}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. This answers what kind of tumour it is; staging answers how far it has spread.
cards.text: The tissue-based classification of a neoplasm records its {{c1::cell or tissue of origin}}.
cards.question: The tissue-based classification of a neoplasm records its {{c1::cell or tissue of origin}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. Benign is not a synonym for cancer. Growth rate alone is not sufficient to decide behaviour.
cards.text: A tumour that does not invade surrounding tissues is classified as {{c1::benign}}.
cards.question: A tumour that does not invade surrounding tissues is classified as {{c1::benign}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. The outlines and figures distinguish malignant infiltration from benign expansile growth.
cards.text: Destructive invasion of surrounding tissue is a defining feature of {{c1::malignancy}}.
cards.question: Destructive invasion of surrounding tissue is a defining feature of {{c1::malignancy}}.

cards.explanation: The figure presents a typical pattern, not an absolute diagnostic rule. Some malignant tumours also grow slowly.
cards.text: The clinical comparison depicts benign tumours as usually {{c1::slow-growing}}.
cards.question: The clinical comparison depicts benign tumours as usually {{c1::slow-growing}}.

cards.explanation: These are comparative clinical clues, not independent proof of malignancy.
cards.text: Ulceration and haemorrhage are described as more frequent in {{c1::malignant}} than benign neoplasms.
cards.question: Ulceration and haemorrhage are described as more frequent in {{c1::malignant}} than benign neoplasms.

cards.explanation: The comparison shows no metastasis for benign tumours. Absence of detected metastases does not prove that a tumour is benign.
cards.text: A discontinuous secondary tumour at a distant site represents {{c1::metastasis}}.
cards.question: A discontinuous secondary tumour at a distant site represents {{c1::metastasis}}.

cards.explanation: The figure notes that benign lesions may be encapsulated; a capsule is not required in every benign tumour.
cards.text: Benign tumours typically have a smooth edge because growth is {{c1::expansile}}.
cards.question: Benign tumours typically have a smooth edge because growth is {{c1::expansile}}.

cards.explanation: Tumour extends into surrounding structures rather than simply pushing them aside.
cards.text: An irregular malignant tumour edge reflects {{c1::infiltrative growth}}.
cards.question: An irregular malignant tumour edge reflects {{c1::infiltrative growth}}.

cards.explanation: The benign comparison is bland and homogeneous.
cards.text: The variegated malignant cut surface in the figure is attributed to haemorrhage and {{c1::necrosis}}.
cards.question: The variegated malignant cut surface in the figure is attributed to haemorrhage and {{c1::necrosis}}.

cards.explanation: The malignant comparison is highly variable, whereas the benign cells are fairly uniform.
cards.text: Marked variation in tumour-cell size and shape is termed {{c1::pleomorphism}}.
cards.question: Marked variation in tumour-cell size and shape is termed {{c1::pleomorphism}}.

cards.explanation: Malignant lesions in the figure often have numerous, sometimes abnormal mitoses; an isolated mitosis alone does not establish malignancy.
cards.text: A tripolar mitosis is an example of an {{c1::abnormal mitotic figure}}.
cards.question: A tripolar mitosis is an example of an {{c1::abnormal mitotic figure}}.

cards.explanation: The diagram also lists perineural invasion; these findings are absent in its benign comparison.
cards.text: Tumour cells within blood vessels or lymphatics demonstrate {{c1::vascular invasion}}.
cards.question: Tumour cells within blood vessels or lymphatics demonstrate {{c1::vascular invasion}}.

cards.explanation: This is an occasional association, not a requirement for every cancer.
cards.text: The microscopic figure notes that {{c1::dysplasia}} may occur in tissue adjacent to a malignancy.
cards.question: The microscopic figure notes that {{c1::dysplasia}} may occur in tissue adjacent to a malignancy.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. The outline subdivides examples by squamous, columnar or transitional epithelium.
cards.text: A benign neoplasm of lining epithelium is called a {{c1::papilloma}}.
cards.question: A benign neoplasm of lining epithelium is called a {{c1::papilloma}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. Contrast adenoma with adenocarcinoma.
cards.text: A benign glandular epithelial tumour is an {{c1::adenoma}}.
cards.question: A benign glandular epithelial tumour is an {{c1::adenoma}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. Squamous, columnar and transitional examples reflect epithelial phenotype.
cards.text: A malignant epithelial tumour is a {{c1::carcinoma}}.
cards.question: A malignant epithelial tumour is a {{c1::carcinoma}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. The glandular component is indicated by adeno-.
cards.text: A malignant gland-forming epithelial tumour is an {{c1::adenocarcinoma}}.
cards.question: A malignant gland-forming epithelial tumour is an {{c1::adenocarcinoma}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. The outline contrasts these with epithelial carcinomas.
cards.text: A malignant tumour of mesenchymal tissues such as bone, cartilage or muscle is a {{c1::sarcoma}}.
cards.question: A malignant tumour of mesenchymal tissues such as bone, cartilage or muscle is a {{c1::sarcoma}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. Lipo- indicates fat; this is a benign -oma example.
cards.text: A benign tumour of adipose tissue is a {{c1::lipoma}}.
cards.question: A benign tumour of adipose tissue is a {{c1::lipoma}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. Fibro- refers to fibrous tissue.
cards.text: A benign tumour of fibrous tissue is a {{c1::fibroma}}.
cards.question: A benign tumour of fibrous tissue is a {{c1::fibroma}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. Contrast the bone prefix with the malignant example osteosarcoma.
cards.text: A benign bone tumour is an {{c1::osteoma}}.
cards.question: A benign bone tumour is an {{c1::osteoma}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. Myo- identifies muscle in the outline’s naming examples.
cards.text: A benign muscle tumour is a {{c1::myoma}}.
cards.question: A benign muscle tumour is a {{c1::myoma}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. The outline groups leukaemias and lymphomas among malignant haematological neoplasms.
cards.text: Malignant blood-forming cancers are called {{c1::leukaemias}}.
cards.question: Malignant blood-forming cancers are called {{c1::leukaemias}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. The -oma ending does not imply benign behaviour in this group.
cards.text: Malignant lymphoid neoplasms are called {{c1::lymphomas}}.
cards.question: Malignant lymphoid neoplasms are called {{c1::lymphomas}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. Do not infer benign behaviour from the suffix alone.
cards.text: Despite its -oma ending, {{c1::melanoma}} is malignant.
cards.question: Despite its -oma ending, {{c1::melanoma}} is malignant.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. Retinoblastoma is its childhood eye-cancer example.
cards.text: The suffix {{c1::-blastoma}} describes tumours resembling embryonic tissue in the outline.
cards.question: The suffix {{c1::-blastoma}} describes tumours resembling embryonic tissue in the outline.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. This illustrates the blastoma naming pattern.
cards.text: Retinoblastoma is the outline’s example of a childhood {{c1::eye}} cancer.
cards.question: Retinoblastoma is the outline’s example of a childhood {{c1::eye}} cancer.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. The outline includes it among tumours named after people.
cards.text: Wilms tumour is a childhood {{c1::kidney}} tumour.
cards.question: Wilms tumour is a childhood {{c1::kidney}} tumour.

cards.explanation: Lecture 1 outline, original p. 1. The eponym does not by itself disclose the tissue of origin.
cards.text: Hodgkin disease belongs to the {{c1::lymphoma}} group.
cards.question: Hodgkin disease belongs to the {{c1::lymphoma}} group.

cards.explanation: This is the meaning labelled on the original vector slide.
cards.text: The tumour-name prefix adeno- denotes {{c1::gland}}.
cards.question: The tumour-name prefix adeno- denotes {{c1::gland}}.

cards.explanation: This is the meaning labelled on the original vector slide.
cards.text: The tumour-name prefix angio- denotes {{c1::vessel, with type unspecified}}.
cards.question: The tumour-name prefix angio- denotes {{c1::vessel, with type unspecified}}.

cards.explanation: This is the meaning labelled on the original vector slide.
cards.text: The tumour-name prefix chondro- denotes {{c1::cartilage}}.
cards.question: The tumour-name prefix chondro- denotes {{c1::cartilage}}.

cards.explanation: This is the meaning labelled on the original vector slide.
cards.text: The tumour-name prefix haemangio- denotes {{c1::blood vessels}}.
cards.question: The tumour-name prefix haemangio- denotes {{c1::blood vessels}}.

cards.explanation: This is the meaning labelled on the original vector slide.
cards.text: The tumour-name prefix lymphangio- denotes {{c1::lymph vessels}}.
cards.question: The tumour-name prefix lymphangio- denotes {{c1::lymph vessels}}.

cards.explanation: This is the meaning labelled on the original vector slide.
cards.text: The tumour-name prefix neuro- denotes {{c1::nerve}}.
cards.question: The tumour-name prefix neuro- denotes {{c1::nerve}}.

cards.text: The slide’s warning-sign list highlights {{c1::a change in usual habits}} involving bowel or bladder function.
cards.question: The slide’s warning-sign list highlights {{c1::a change in usual habits}} involving bowel or bladder function.

cards.explanation: This is a nonspecific warning sign warranting assessment, not evidence that a person definitely has cancer.
cards.text: The slide’s warning-sign list highlights {{c1::failure to heal}} involving a skin sore.
cards.question: The slide’s warning-sign list highlights {{c1::failure to heal}} involving a skin sore.

cards.text: The slide’s warning-sign list highlights {{c1::an unusual occurrence}} involving bleeding or discharge.
cards.question: The slide’s warning-sign list highlights {{c1::an unusual occurrence}} involving bleeding or discharge.

cards.question: The slide’s warning-sign list highlights {{c1::a new thickening or lump}} involving a breast or another body region.

cards.question: The slide’s warning-sign list highlights {{c1::an obvious change}} involving a pre-existing wart or mole.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. The outline describes this as direct spread, often along a path of least resistance.
cards.text: Spread directly into adjacent tissues is {{c1::local invasion}}.
cards.question: Spread directly into adjacent tissues is {{c1::local invasion}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. This is a broad tendency, not an exclusive route. Carcinomas can also spread haematogenously; melanoma is not a carcinoma despite being placed beside it in the outline.
cards.text: Many carcinomas initially spread through {{c1::lymphatic vessels}}.
cards.question: Many carcinomas initially spread through {{c1::lymphatic vessels}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. Osteosarcoma is the outline’s example. This is a tendency rather than an absolute separation from lymphatic spread.
cards.text: A typical vascular route highlighted for sarcomas is spread through {{c1::blood vessels}}.
cards.question: A typical vascular route highlighted for sarcomas is spread through {{c1::blood vessels}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. This is a separate route from blood-borne or lymphatic dissemination.
cards.text: Spread across a body cavity such as the peritoneal cavity is {{c1::transcoelomic spread}}.
cards.question: Spread across a body cavity such as the peritoneal cavity is {{c1::transcoelomic spread}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. It describes stomach or colon cancer extending through the gut wall and disseminating in that cavity.
cards.text: The outline’s example of transcoelomic spread involves gastrointestinal cancer reaching the {{c1::ovaries}} via the peritoneal cavity.
cards.question: The outline’s example of transcoelomic spread involves gastrointestinal cancer reaching the {{c1::ovaries}} via the peritoneal cavity.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. The outline lists loss of junctional complexes and adhesion proteins as contributors.
cards.text: Detachment from the primary tumour is facilitated by reduced {{c1::cell–cell adhesion}}.
cards.question: Detachment from the primary tumour is facilitated by reduced {{c1::cell–cell adhesion}}.

cards.explanation: The figure contrasts connected normal epithelial cells with separated malignant cells. Not all malignancies lose E-cadherin.
cards.text: Downregulation of {{c1::E-cadherin}} reduces cohesion between neighbouring tumour cells.
cards.question: Downregulation of {{c1::E-cadherin}} reduces cohesion between neighbouring tumour cells.

cards.explanation: The figure labels an autocrine motility factor.
cards.text: A motility factor made by the tumour cell and acting back on that cell uses an {{c1::autocrine}} pathway.
cards.question: A motility factor made by the tumour cell and acting back on that cell uses an {{c1::autocrine}} pathway.

cards.explanation: The signal originates from a neighbouring stromal cell rather than the responding tumour cell.
cards.text: The fibroblast-derived scatter factor in the diagram stimulates tumour cells through a {{c1::paracrine}} pathway.
cards.question: The fibroblast-derived scatter factor in the diagram stimulates tumour cells through a {{c1::paracrine}} pathway.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. The outline names collagenases, gelatinases and stromelysins.
cards.text: The enzymes used to break down basement membrane and extracellular matrix are {{c1::proteolytic enzymes}}.
cards.question: The enzymes used to break down basement membrane and extracellular matrix are {{c1::proteolytic enzymes}}.

cards.explanation: The figure distinguishes laminin, its receptor and type IV collagen.
cards.text: The basement-membrane component bound by the receptor in the diagram is {{c1::laminin}}.
cards.question: The basement-membrane component bound by the receptor in the diagram is {{c1::laminin}}.

cards.explanation: This is the type shown in the supplied invasion diagram.
cards.text: The collagen type labelled in the basement membrane is {{c1::type IV collagen}}.
cards.question: The collagen type labelled in the basement membrane is {{c1::type IV collagen}}.

cards.explanation: Proteolytic destruction helps the cell traverse the matrix barrier.
cards.text: The tumour-cell enzymes labelled as disrupting basement membrane are {{c1::metalloproteinases}}.
cards.question: The tumour-cell enzymes labelled as disrupting basement membrane are {{c1::metalloproteinases}}.

cards.explanation: The image labels integrin binding to the RGD sequence on fibronectin.
cards.text: The cell-surface receptors shown binding fibronectin during migration are {{c1::integrins}}.
cards.question: The cell-surface receptors shown binding fibronectin during migration are {{c1::integrins}}.

cards.explanation: This is the sequence explicitly labelled on the slide; its amino-acid expansion is not required to read the figure.
cards.text: The fibronectin sequence recognised in the integrin-binding diagram is {{c1::RGD}}.
cards.question: The fibronectin sequence recognised in the integrin-binding diagram is {{c1::RGD}}.

cards.explanation: Do not treat it as interchangeable with E-cadherin-mediated cell–cell adhesion. Matrix attachment can aid migration even when cell–cell cohesion is reduced.
cards.text: Fibronectin provides a cell–{{c1::extracellular matrix}} adhesion interaction in the migration diagram.
cards.question: Fibronectin provides a cell–{{c1::extracellular matrix}} adhesion interaction in the migration diagram.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. The outline describes vessel invasion after destruction of the vascular basement membrane.
cards.text: Entry of tumour cells into blood or lymphatic vessels is {{c1::intravasation}}.
cards.question: Entry of tumour cells into blood or lymphatic vessels is {{c1::intravasation}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. Contrast exit with intravasation, the earlier entry step.
cards.text: Exit of tumour cells from a vessel at a secondary site is {{c1::extravasation}}.
cards.question: Exit of tumour cells from a vessel at a secondary site is {{c1::extravasation}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. The outline specifically includes survival against host defences. Reaching a vessel does not guarantee successful metastasis.
cards.text: After extravasation, cells must {{c1::survive at the new site}} before a secondary tumour can grow.
cards.question: After extravasation, cells must {{c1::survive at the new site}} before a secondary tumour can grow.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. This follows survival and colonisation, rather than merely transport in the circulation.
cards.text: Growth of a detached secondary tumour requires {{c1::proliferation at the distant site}}.
cards.question: Growth of a detached secondary tumour requires {{c1::proliferation at the distant site}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. The outline names this as an example, not the only possible metastatic site.
cards.text: The distant spread example given for colorectal cancer is spread to the {{c1::liver}}.
cards.question: The distant spread example given for colorectal cancer is spread to the {{c1::liver}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. This does not establish the brain as the most frequent metastatic destination for every lung cancer.
cards.text: The outline gives lung cancer spreading through blood to the {{c1::brain}} as an example.
cards.question: The outline gives lung cancer spreading through blood to the {{c1::brain}} as an example.

cards.explanation: The diagram depicts one progression pathway; it does not imply that every adenoma inevitably becomes malignant.
cards.text: The final adenoma–carcinoma panel shows invasion beyond the {{c1::basement membrane}}.
cards.question: The final adenoma–carcinoma panel shows invasion beyond the {{c1::basement membrane}}.

cards.explanation: The following panel shows invasion of underlying connective tissue.
cards.text: Carcinoma in situ remains above an {{c1::intact basement membrane}}.
cards.question: Carcinoma in situ remains above an {{c1::intact basement membrane}}.

cards.explanation: The diagram separates connective-tissue invasion from subsequent vascular entry.
cards.text: Stromal invasion is distinct from entry into {{c1::blood or lymphatic vessels}}.
cards.question: Stromal invasion is distinct from entry into {{c1::blood or lymphatic vessels}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. Classification describes tumour type or origin. The outline’s first practice MCQ tests this distinction.
cards.text: Clinical staging describes the {{c1::extent of cancer spread}} at diagnosis.
cards.question: Clinical staging describes the {{c1::extent of cancer spread}} at diagnosis.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. Its precise meaning depends on the organ-specific staging system.
cards.text: In TNM, T describes the {{c1::primary tumour}}.
cards.question: In TNM, T describes the {{c1::primary tumour}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. It does not describe distant metastases.
cards.text: In TNM, N describes {{c1::regional lymph node involvement}}.
cards.question: In TNM, N describes {{c1::regional lymph node involvement}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. Regional nodes are represented by N, not M.
cards.text: In TNM, M describes {{c1::distant metastasis}}.
cards.question: In TNM, M describes {{c1::distant metastasis}}.

cards.explanation: Correction: Lecture 2 outline incorrectly treats Tis and T0 as equivalent. The slide table correctly labels Tis as carcinoma in situ.
cards.text: The designation for carcinoma in situ is {{c1::Tis}}.
cards.question: The designation for carcinoma in situ is {{c1::Tis}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. This corrects the outline’s conflation of T0 with Tis. The two categories are not interchangeable.
cards.text: T0 means {{c1::no evidence of a primary tumour}}, rather than carcinoma in situ.
cards.question: T0 means {{c1::no evidence of a primary tumour}}, rather than carcinoma in situ.
cards.answer: no evidence of a primary tumour

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 1. N0 is a nodal category, not proof that the primary tumour is non-invasive.
cards.text: N0 indicates {{c1::no regional lymph node metastasis}}.
cards.question: N0 indicates {{c1::no regional lymph node metastasis}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 2. The M category is separate from local extent and regional nodes.
cards.text: M0 indicates {{c1::no distant metastasis identified}}.
cards.question: M0 indicates {{c1::no distant metastasis identified}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 2. M1 does not specify the primary tumour’s size.
cards.text: M1 indicates {{c1::distant metastasis present}}.
cards.question: M1 indicates {{c1::distant metastasis present}}.

cards.explanation: This layered anatomy provides the basis for colorectal depth-of-invasion staging.
cards.text: The wall layer between the mucosa and muscularis externa is the {{c1::submucosa}}.
cards.question: The wall layer between the mucosa and muscularis externa is the {{c1::submucosa}}.

cards.explanation: The label helps explain why depth of invasion relates to access to routes of spread.
cards.text: The major blood and lymphatic vessels indicated in the wall diagram lie in the {{c1::submucosa}}.
cards.question: The major blood and lymphatic vessels indicated in the wall diagram lie in the {{c1::submucosa}}.

cards.explanation: The diagram labels an inner circular and outer longitudinal layer.
cards.text: The outer muscle layer of muscularis externa is {{c1::longitudinal}}.
cards.question: The outer muscle layer of muscularis externa is {{c1::longitudinal}}.

cards.explanation: Distinguish this thin mucosal layer from the deeper muscularis externa involved in T2 staging.
cards.text: The muscle layer forming part of the mucosa is the {{c1::muscularis mucosae}}.
cards.question: The muscle layer forming part of the mucosa is the {{c1::muscularis mucosae}}.

cards.explanation: Both structures are labelled in the supplied large-bowel overview.
cards.text: The rectum continues distally into the {{c1::anal canal}}.
cards.question: The rectum continues distally into the {{c1::anal canal}}.

cards.explanation: Depth of invasion, rather than diameter alone, defines this colorectal category.
cards.text: A colorectal tumour invading the submucosa is {{c1::T1}}.
cards.question: A colorectal tumour invading the submucosa is {{c1::T1}}.

cards.explanation: The source table describes invasion into the underlying muscular layer. This is not the muscularis mucosae.
cards.text: A colorectal tumour invading the muscularis propria is {{c1::T2}}.
cards.question: A colorectal tumour invading the muscularis propria is {{c1::T2}}.

cards.explanation: The source table abbreviates this as invasion through the muscular layer.
cards.text: Colorectal invasion through the muscularis propria into pericolorectal tissue is {{c1::T3}}.
cards.question: Colorectal invasion through the muscularis propria into pericolorectal tissue is {{c1::T3}}.

cards.explanation: The old slide compresses this category; contemporary staging distinguishes T4a and T4b. Free peritoneal tumour deposits are a different finding.
cards.text: Colorectal invasion of the visceral peritoneal surface or adjacent organs corresponds to {{c1::T4}}.
cards.question: Colorectal invasion of the visceral peritoneal surface or adjacent organs corresponds to {{c1::T4}}.

cards.explanation: This is the table’s simplified numerical distinction. Modern colorectal staging also includes N1c and more detailed subcategories.
cards.text: The older table assigns one to three positive regional nodes to {{c1::N1}}.
cards.question: The older table assigns one to three positive regional nodes to {{c1::N1}}.

cards.explanation: This is the broad numerical division shown; modern classifications subdivide N2.
cards.text: The older table assigns four or more positive regional nodes to {{c1::N2}}.
cards.question: The older table assigns four or more positive regional nodes to {{c1::N2}}.

cards.explanation: Modern colorectal TNM does not use N3. Do not apply the old named-vascular-trunk row as a current colorectal staging rule.
cards.text: The slide’s colorectal N3 category should be treated as {{c1::historical staging terminology}}.
cards.question: The slide’s colorectal N3 category should be treated as {{c1::historical staging terminology}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 2. Interpret each component independently instead of equating a locally advanced primary with distant spread.
cards.text: T3N0M0 represents local extension through the muscular layer, with no regional node involvement and {{c1::no distant metastasis identified}}.
cards.question: T3N0M0 represents local extension through the muscular layer, with no regional node involvement and {{c1::no distant metastasis identified}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 2. T4 describes local extent; M0 indicates that distant metastasis has not been identified.
cards.text: In T4N1M0, the N1 component records {{c1::regional lymph node involvement}}.
cards.question: In T4N1M0, the N1 component records {{c1::regional lymph node involvement}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 2. Only the M category changes; M1 is the distant-metastasis marker.
cards.text: Of T4N1M0 and T4N1M1, the code showing distant spread is {{c1::T4N1M1}}.
cards.question: Of T4N1M0 and T4N1M1, the code showing distant spread is {{c1::T4N1M1}}.

cards.question: In the outline’s illustrative table, T1/T2N0M0 is paired with a five-year survival of {{c1::90%}}.

cards.question: In the outline’s illustrative table, T3N0M0 is paired with a five-year survival of {{c1::80%}}.

cards.explanation: Lecture 2 outline, original p. 2. This is a lecture-specific teaching value, not a current individual prognosis. No population, date or evidence source is supplied for the survival estimates.

cards.question: In the outline’s illustrative table, T4N0M0 is paired with a five-year survival of {{c1::60–70%}}.

slides.text:
The slide’s warning-sign list highlights {{c1::a change in usual habits}} involving bowel or bladder function.
The slide’s warning-sign list highlights {{c1::failure to heal}} involving a skin sore.
The slide’s warning-sign list highlights {{c1::an unusual occurrence}} involving bleeding or discharge.
The slide’s warning-sign list highlights {{c1::a new thickening or lump}} involving a breast or another body region.
The slide’s warning-sign list highlights {{c1::difficulty swallowing}} involving swallowing.
The slide’s warning-sign list highlights {{c1::an obvious change}} involving a pre-existing wart or mole.
The slide’s warning-sign list highlights {{c1::persistent hoarseness or a nagging cough}} involving voice or respiratory symptoms.

The clinical comparison depicts benign tumours as usually {{c1::slow-growing}}.
Ulceration and haemorrhage are described as more frequent in {{c1::malignant}} than benign neoplasms.
A discontinuous secondary tumour at a distant site represents {{c1::metastasis}}.

Benign tumours typically have a smooth edge because growth is {{c1::expansile}}.
An irregular malignant tumour edge reflects {{c1::infiltrative growth}}.
The variegated malignant cut surface in the figure is attributed to haemorrhage and {{c1::necrosis}}.

Marked variation in tumour-cell size and shape is termed {{c1::pleomorphism}}.
A tripolar mitosis is an example of an {{c1::abnormal mitotic figure}}.
Tumour cells within blood vessels or lymphatics demonstrate {{c1::vascular invasion}}.
The microscopic figure notes that {{c1::dysplasia}} may occur in tissue adjacent to a malignancy.

The tumour-name prefix adeno- denotes {{c1::gland}}.
The tumour-name prefix angio- denotes {{c1::vessel, with type unspecified}}.
The tumour-name prefix chondro- denotes {{c1::cartilage}}.
The tumour-name prefix haemangio- denotes {{c1::blood vessels}}.
The tumour-name prefix lymphangio- denotes {{c1::lymph vessels}}.
The tumour-name prefix neuro- denotes {{c1::nerve}}.
Downregulation of {{c1::E-cadherin}} reduces cohesion between neighbouring tumour cells.

A motility factor made by the tumour cell and acting back on that cell uses an {{c1::autocrine}} pathway.
The fibroblast-derived scatter factor in the diagram stimulates tumour cells through a {{c1::paracrine}} pathway.
The final adenoma–carcinoma panel shows invasion beyond the {{c1::basement membrane}}.

Carcinoma in situ remains above an {{c1::intact basement membrane}}.
Stromal invasion is distinct from entry into {{c1::blood or lymphatic vessels}}.

The basement-membrane component bound by the receptor in the diagram is {{c1::laminin}}.
The collagen type labelled in the basement membrane is {{c1::type IV collagen}}.
The tumour-cell enzymes labelled as disrupting basement membrane are {{c1::metalloproteinases}}.

The cell-surface receptors shown binding fibronectin during migration are {{c1::integrins}}.
The fibronectin sequence recognised in the integrin-binding diagram is {{c1::RGD}}.
Fibronectin provides a cell–{{c1::extracellular matrix}} adhesion interaction in the migration diagram.
The rectum continues distally into the {{c1::anal canal}}.

The wall layer between the mucosa and muscularis externa is the {{c1::submucosa}}.
The major blood and lymphatic vessels indicated in the wall diagram lie in the {{c1::submucosa}}.
The outer muscle layer of muscularis externa is {{c1::longitudinal}}.
The muscle layer forming part of the mucosa is the {{c1::muscularis mucosae}}.

The designation for carcinoma in situ is {{c1::Tis}}.
A colorectal tumour invading the submucosa is {{c1::T1}}.
A colorectal tumour invading the muscularis propria is {{c1::T2}}.
Colorectal invasion through the muscularis propria into pericolorectal tissue is {{c1::T3}}.
Colorectal invasion of the visceral peritoneal surface or adjacent organs corresponds to {{c1::T4}}.
The older table assigns one to three positive regional nodes to {{c1::N1}}.
The older table assigns four or more positive regional nodes to {{c1::N2}}.
The slide’s colorectal N3 category should be treated as {{c1::historical staging terminology}}.

Cancer is characterised by {{c1::unregulated cell proliferation}}.
Normal cell turnover maintains a functional {{c1::steady state}}.
Cancer cells may become less dependent on external {{c1::growth factors}}.
Failure to stop proliferating when cells contact neighbours is loss of {{c1::contact inhibition}}.
Growth without the normal requirement for attachment to a substrate is loss of {{c1::anchorage dependence}}.
Reduced resemblance to the specialised tissue of origin is loss of {{c1::differentiation}}.
Cancer is a family of diseases with different treatment responses and {{c1::clinical outcomes}}.
One basis for classifying neoplasms is their biological {{c1::behaviour}}.
The tissue-based classification of a neoplasm records its {{c1::cell or tissue of origin}}.
A tumour that does not invade surrounding tissues is classified as {{c1::benign}}.
Destructive invasion of surrounding tissue is a defining feature of {{c1::malignancy}}.
A benign neoplasm of lining epithelium is called a {{c1::papilloma}}.
A benign glandular epithelial tumour is an {{c1::adenoma}}.
A malignant epithelial tumour is a {{c1::carcinoma}}.
A malignant gland-forming epithelial tumour is an {{c1::adenocarcinoma}}.
A malignant tumour of mesenchymal tissues such as bone, cartilage or muscle is a {{c1::sarcoma}}.
A benign tumour of adipose tissue is a {{c1::lipoma}}.
A benign tumour of fibrous tissue is a {{c1::fibroma}}.
A benign bone tumour is an {{c1::osteoma}}.
A benign muscle tumour is a {{c1::myoma}}.
Malignant blood-forming cancers are called {{c1::leukaemias}}.
Malignant lymphoid neoplasms are called {{c1::lymphomas}}.
Despite its -oma ending, {{c1::melanoma}} is malignant.
The suffix {{c1::-blastoma}} describes tumours resembling embryonic tissue in the outline.
Retinoblastoma is the outline’s example of a childhood {{c1::eye}} cancer.
Wilms tumour is a childhood {{c1::kidney}} tumour.
Hodgkin disease belongs to the {{c1::lymphoma}} group.

Spread directly into adjacent tissues is {{c1::local invasion}}.
Many carcinomas initially spread through {{c1::lymphatic vessels}}.
A typical vascular route highlighted for sarcomas is spread through {{c1::blood vessels}}.
Spread across a body cavity such as the peritoneal cavity is {{c1::transcoelomic spread}}.
The outline’s example of transcoelomic spread involves gastrointestinal cancer reaching the {{c1::ovaries}} via the peritoneal cavity.
Detachment from the primary tumour is facilitated by reduced {{c1::cell–cell adhesion}}.
The enzymes used to break down basement membrane and extracellular matrix are {{c1::proteolytic enzymes}}.
Entry of tumour cells into blood or lymphatic vessels is {{c1::intravasation}}.
Exit of tumour cells from a vessel at a secondary site is {{c1::extravasation}}.
After extravasation, cells must {{c1::survive at the new site}} before a secondary tumour can grow.
Growth of a detached secondary tumour requires {{c1::proliferation at the distant site}}.
The distant spread example given for colorectal cancer is spread to the {{c1::liver}}.
The outline gives lung cancer spreading through blood to the {{c1::brain}} as an example.
Clinical staging describes the {{c1::extent of cancer spread}} at diagnosis.
In TNM, T describes the {{c1::primary tumour}}.
In TNM, N describes {{c1::regional lymph node involvement}}.
In TNM, M describes {{c1::distant metastasis}}.
T0 means {{c1::no evidence of a primary tumour}}, rather than carcinoma in situ.
N0 indicates {{c1::no regional lymph node metastasis}}.

M0 indicates {{c1::no distant metastasis identified}}.
M1 indicates {{c1::distant metastasis present}}.
T3N0M0 represents local extension through the muscular layer, with no regional node involvement and {{c1::no distant metastasis identified}}.
In T4N1M0, the N1 component records {{c1::regional lymph node involvement}}.
Of T4N1M0 and T4N1M1, the code showing distant spread is {{c1::T4N1M1}}.
In the outline’s illustrative table, T1/T2N0M0 is paired with a five-year survival of {{c1::90%}}.
In the outline’s illustrative table, T3N0M0 is paired with a five-year survival of {{c1::80%}}.
In the outline’s illustrative table, T4N0M0 is paired with a five-year survival of {{c1::60–70%}}.
In the outline’s illustrative table, T3N1M0 is paired with a five-year survival of {{c1::50%}}.
In the outline’s illustrative table, T4N1M0 is paired with a five-year survival of {{c1::40%}}.
In the outline’s illustrative table, T4N1M1 is paired with a five-year survival of {{c1::less than 30%}}.
For the outline’s T4N0M0 practice question, the offered answer matching its 60–70% range is {{c1::70%}}.
A tumour cell entering the circulation does not necessarily form a metastasis because it must also survive, extravasate and {{c1::establish growth at a secondary site}}.
The transcoelomic route shows that distant spread is not restricted to {{c1::blood and lymphatic vessels}}.
The vascular route taken by disseminating cells can influence {{c1::which organs they encounter}}.
